title: How songs got titled and how arrangements worked
summary: Titles came later from the office; Ellington cued tunes with a few bars, and arrangements were skeletons with solos left to the soloist.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: And then in New York you recorded quite frequently?
Oh, everytime you looked up you were recording.
And you were saying that you didn't always know the name of what you were playing, because it was named later by whom?

The lyricist, or whoever wrote the lyrics to it, if there were lyrics. They would decide what to call this number, and we'd hear it later on. But we didn't pay any attention to names, because when we played, they didn't call the name of the music. All Ellington would do was strike out the first few bars, or so. Some progressions and we'd know what that number was. So we never paid any attention to names.
There was never anything written down?

Yes. There were sort of skeleton arrangements. The solos weren't written. It was like, say the next 32 bars of Cootie, or Brown, or Johnny Hodges, or like that. That's the way it was on the arrangements. No one wrote any solos for anybody.
You never did with Ellington, did you?
It was always left up to the artist to solo?
Yes. You make up your own. This is the background, put the solo to it, see.
